oil.summary: Crude staged a dramatic intraday reversal, with WTI settling at $96.31/bbl (-7.50%) and Brent at $104.15/bbl (-11.47%), the sharpest single-day drops in recent memory. The catalyst was a joint US-Iran signal that diplomatic channels remain open, unwinding a significant portion of the geopolitical war premium that had built following Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery last week. RBOB gasoline led the sell-off at -12.44%, reflecting the same risk-off unwind in refined products. Offsetting factors kept declines from deepening further: Ukraine defied Washington by resuming strikes on Russian refineries—hitting at least three facilities since Friday, including a reported fire at a major Volga hub—and a sanctioned Iranian tanker successfully delivered LNG cargo to China despite the US naval blockade. ADNOC's chief warned that global supply buffers have been severely eroded. Options markets now price a 77% chance of an OPEC cut at the May 2026 meeting.
drivers: US-Iran diplomatic signals triggered a sharp unwind of the geopolitical war premium, driving WTI -7.5% and Brent -11.5% on the day
Ukraine resumed and escalated strikes on Russian refineries (three hits since Friday), providing a partial supply-risk floor under prices
CME options now price a 77% probability of an OPEC production cut at the next meeting (May 3, 2026), reflecting underlying demand concern

gas.summary: Henry Hub eased modestly to $2.869/MMBtu (-1.00% on the day) but remains up over 10% on the week, suggesting near-term bullish momentum despite today's soft session. TTF fell sharply, -10.10% to €93.45/MWh, likely tracking the broader crude and geopolitical-premium unwind after US-Iran diplomacy headlines, though TTF remains up 25% on the month—a sign of persistent European tightness. On the structural side, two sizable LNG investment deals headlined the session: Blackstone-led investors acquired a $3.1 billion stake in LNG Canada, and a US-backed consortium proposed a $4.4 billion LNG import terminal in Pakistan, signaling continued global appetite for long-term LNG infrastructure. News flow on gas fundamentals was otherwise thin today.
drivers: TTF dropped 10% on the day, likely tracking the crude geopolitical-premium unwind, though the month-to-date gain of 25% signals persistent European supply tightness
Blackstone and Canadian institutional investors closed a $3.1 billion stake purchase in LNG Canada, reinforcing long-term export capacity build-out
A US-backed consortium proposed a $4.4 billion LNG import terminal in Pakistan, reflecting growing emerging-market demand for seaborne LNG

power.summary: EU carbon allowances (EUA) bucked the broader energy sell-off, edging up +1.49% to $86.145/EUA and extending a month-to-date gain of 7.38%—a notable divergence from the sharp declines in crude and TTF. The EUA resilience likely reflects structural compliance demand that is less sensitive to short-term geopolitical swings. The key macro backdrop for European power remains the Strait of Hormuz situation: Iran offered to reopen the strait within two days conditional on US concessions, though separate headlines indicated Iran rejected US peace talks, leaving the situation fluid. Central Asia faces a distinct but parallel stress test, with reports flagging rising concern over the region's capacity to generate sufficient heat and electricity ahead of winter. Dedicated power and carbon headline flow was thin today; the sector is largely trading in the shadow of the oil and gas volatility.
drivers: EUA carbon prices rose +1.49% and are up 7.38% on the month, showing resilience against the broader energy commodity sell-off driven by compliance-floor demand
Iran's conditional offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz introduces uncertainty around European energy security and power generation feedstock costs
Central Asia's power grid is flagged as a stress point heading into winter, with insufficient generation capacity a growing concern for the region
